subtopic: Facing peer pressure to do something unsafe
subtype: Approach: assuming everyone else is comfortable [Pitfall]
passage: Keerthana, your Tanuja Nani once had a brother, Mahesh, and this is about the canal. He was fifteen. After the first rains, four friends said, "Let's swim at the sluice." Mahesh's stomach turned over, because he had seen how the water ran that week. But everyone was nodding and Ravi was already pulling off his shirt, so Mahesh thought, they all want this, and said nothing. Ravi slipped at the edge and the current took him ten feet before a fisherman waded in and dragged him out, coughing. They ran home in silence. Years later at a wedding, Mahesh said, "I never wanted to go." Kishan said, "Neither did I." And Ravi said, "I was only showing off because I thought you all wanted to." Three of them, one belief nobody had checked.

qa.q: Where did the friends want to swim?
qa.a: The friends wanted to swim at the sluice.

qa.q: What did Mahesh believe about the others, and what did he feel?
qa.a: Mahesh believed everyone wanted to go, though his stomach turned over, so he felt uneasy but stayed silent.

qa.q: At what moment could Mahesh have changed the outcome, and how?
qa.a: When his stomach turned over, he could have said 'I'm not sure about this,' because others who felt uneasy might have agreed.

qa.q: What was Ravi's view of what the group wanted?
qa.a: Ravi believed the others wanted to swim and was showing off for them, when in fact they felt uneasy too.

grounding: The student assumes all others want to do it and stays silent, and later learns several felt uneasy too, showing how a false belief in group agreement keeps everyone quiet.

subtopic: Facing peer pressure to do something unsafe
subtype: Approach: assuming everyone else is comfortable [Pitfall]
passage: On the second night of the school trip to Nainital, someone whispered that the whole dorm was sneaking out to the lake at midnight. Siddharth lay on his bunk, stomach tight. The lake was dark, the road was steep, and the teachers would be furious. But everyone else seemed so keen. So when the torches came on at midnight, he pulled on his shoes and followed without a word. It was cold, a boy slipped on the wet steps and grazed his knee, and a teacher's torch found them by the jetty. All eight were marched back, and their parents were phoned in the morning. On the bus home Anand, who had walked beside him the whole way, said quietly, "I hated every second of that." Two more boys nodded. Siddharth stared at him. "Me too. Why didn't anyone say?"

qa.q: Where was the dorm sneaking out to?
How did Siddharth feel lying on his bunk?
qa.a: He felt anxious, stomach tight, worried about the dark lake, the steep road and the teachers' anger.

qa.q: What might have happened if Siddharth had spoken up?
qa.a: Anand and the others who also hated it might have joined him, and the group could have stayed in, since several already felt the same.

qa.q: What was the walk like for Anand?
qa.a: Anand hated every second but stayed silent too, believing the others wanted to go.

grounding: Shows a student staying silent because he assumes everyone wants to go, then learning several others felt uneasy too.

subtopic: Facing peer pressure to do something unsafe
subtype: Approach: assuming everyone else is comfortable [Pitfall]
passage: Behind the tuition building in Pune, Rishi pulled out a packet of cigarettes he had taken from his cousin. "Everyone's trying one. Right?" Nilesh felt his throat tighten. He didn't want to. But Anand was already nodding, the others were crowding in, and nobody said anything, so Nilesh assumed he was the only one who minded. He took one, coughed until his eyes watered, and went home smelling of smoke. His mother noticed at dinner, and they talked for a long time. The next day, waiting for the bus, Anand said, "Honestly, I only nodded because everyone else looked fine with it." Farid added, "I almost threw up." Nilesh laughed, then stopped. Five of them had stood there, and at least three had wanted to say no.

qa.q: Where did Rishi get the cigarettes?
Why did Nilesh go along even though he didn't want to?
qa.a: He felt uneasy and alone, assuming he was the only one who minded because nobody else spoke.

qa.q: What could Nilesh do the next time he feels this way?
qa.a: Say a simple "I'm out" early, since others who feel the same will often join once one person speaks.

qa.q: How did Anand see the moment behind the building?
qa.a: Anand only nodded because everyone else looked fine, so Anand felt uneasy too but hid it.

grounding: Shows a student staying quiet because he believes everyone agrees, then learning most of the group felt uneasy too.
